questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Chinese entry into the Korean War
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the stated justification for Chinese intervention in Korea
questions.stem: A revision group reopens the question of why Chinese forces entered the war in late 1950, after months of fighting had already begun. Which reading of the decision is best supported?

options.text: China publicly framed its entry as a delayed, defensive response to border attacks and appeals for help
China entered in order to guarantee a permanent partition of the peninsula at the 38th parallel
options.misconception: Reads a defensive justification as a partition scheme

options.text: China entered only after signing a treaty that bound it to fight beside the United Nations forces
options.misconception: Invents a treaty commitment China did not make

options.text: China's entry was wholly unplanned, and its leaders had not chosen to intervene before the crossing
options.misconception: Treats a documented prior decision as spontaneous action

questions.explanation: China's public account cited border attacks and appeals for assistance, and it delayed its arrival until those appeals were made, which preserved a defensive claim. It was neither a bargain with the United Nations nor an unplanned reaction.
questions.hint: Ask what the stated reasons were and when the forces arrived.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Reason about why a negotiated line was accepted rather than a decisive outcome
questions.stem: In a study session, the group asks why the fighting stopped at a negotiated line rather than continuing until one side won outright. Which inference is best supported?

options.text: Because neither side would pay the continuing cost, so the line froze a stalemate in place
Because the general assembly had already voted by a large majority to end the war outright
options.misconception: Invents an assembly vote that ended the fighting

options.text: Because the northern government had been persuaded to surrender its weapons for good
options.misconception: Overstates the terms of the armistice agreement

options.text: Because the southern government had been promised the whole peninsula by a later accord
options.misconception: Describes a later agreement as the cause of the truce

questions.explanation: A negotiated line is what two governments accept when neither can force its aims at an acceptable price, so the armistice froze the situation rather than settling it. No assembly vote, disarmament, or territorial promise is needed to explain it.
questions.hint: Ask what both sides gained by stopping where they were.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compute the difference between a requested and an authorized military figure
questions.stem: A study handout sets out three budget figures for one year of war costs: the administration requested 7.5 billion dollars, the military leadership asked for 11.0 billion, and the legislature authorized 9.2 billion. By how much did the authorized figure exceed the request?

options.text: 1.7 billion dollars, since 9.2 minus 7.5 leaves 1.7
3.5 billion dollars, since 11.0 minus 7.5 leaves 3.5
options.misconception: Compares the military request with the civilian request instead

options.text: 1.8 billion dollars, since 11.0 minus 9.2 leaves 1.8
options.misconception: Compares the military request with the authorized figure instead

options.text: 27.7 billion dollars, since the three amounts should be added together
options.misconception: Adds the three amounts instead of finding one difference

questions.explanation: The authorized figure exceeded the request by 9.2 minus 7.5, which is 1.7 billion dollars. The other pairings answer different questions, and adding the three amounts produces a total that was never asked for.
questions.hint: Subtract the requested amount from the authorized amount.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the pattern in a sequence of escalating military measures

stimulus.body: The document lists the steps in order: advisers were sent first, then a bombing campaign against the north began, then large ground deployments followed, then the bombing campaign was widened, and finally further ground units were added. A later line notes that the earlier measures were not withdrawn as the later ones were adopted.

questions.stem: What pattern does the sequence show?

options.text: Each step added another instrument of pressure while the earlier measures continued in place
Each step replaced the earlier method, so only the newest instrument was in use at any time
options.misconception: Reads escalation as substitution rather than addition

options.text: The steps were decided in the reverse order and only then put into effect
options.misconception: Reverses the order in which the steps were taken

options.text: The steps show a policy fixed at the start and merely timed differently as the war went on
options.misconception: Assumes a fixed policy with only different timing

questions.explanation: The list shows measures accumulating rather than replacing one another, and the closing line makes clear that earlier instruments were kept. That combination is the defining feature of escalation carried out in steps.
questions.hint: Ask what happened to the earlier measures as new ones were added.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the political expectations attached to bombing the north
questions.stem: The revision notes ask the student to explain why bombing the north was expected to produce political results rather than merely military damage. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: Air power was expected to work by damaging the industrial base of the north so that the country's war effort would lose the supplies it depended on, and by demonstrating to the government in the south that no price would be spared. Officials hoped that visible destruction would convince the north that the war could not be won, and the campaign was also read abroad as a sign of resolve that would reassure allies. The expectation was that pressure of this kind would change the calculation of leaders who had judged fighting on cheaper than conceding.

questions.explanation: A good answer links damage to supply, supply to the war effort, and the war effort to leaders' calculations, and it notes the effect expected on allies. It should not treat the expected outcome as evidence about what followed.
questions.hint: Ask how material damage was supposed to change a decision.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compare two kinds of casualty figure used in a war
questions.stem: One revision exercise compares two ways of measuring the human cost of a war: a count of bodies recovered at one point in the fighting, and a total estimated loss for the whole conflict. Which combined judgment is most accurate?

options.text: A recovered-body count covers one place and time, while a total estimate spans the conflict and other causes
A recovered-body count gives the complete figure, while a total estimate understates the loss
options.misconception: Reverses which measure gives the fuller picture

options.text: Both measures are equally reliable, because they rest on the same body of evidence
options.misconception: Assumes one set of evidence produces both figures identically

options.text: Neither measure is usable, because a reliable count of war deaths cannot be produced
options.misconception: Overstates the uselessness of contested estimates

questions.explanation: A body count is a snapshot of one place and time and usually captures only what could be recovered, while a total estimate attempts to cover the whole conflict including deaths from disease and other causes. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions and carry different gaps.
questions.hint: Ask what each measure covers and what it leaves out.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why control of appropriations gave civilians leverage over plans
questions.stem: A revision group asks what made the power over the military purse so effective during a long war. Which explanation is best?

options.text: Funds had to be renewed on a schedule, which gave civilian bodies recurring chances to withhold or condition money
A single appropriation could never be revisited once the legislature had voted it
options.misconception: Treats appropriations as fixed once granted

options.text: The executive could not request money at all without the military leadership's approval first
options.misconception: Assigns the initiative to the military rather than the executive

options.text: War funding sat outside the ordinary budget process, so no civilian body could reach it
options.misconception: Contradicts the recurring review that made the power work

questions.explanation: Because money for a war had to be voted again, civilian officials gained leverage at every renewal, which is what allowed them to slow a campaign or attach conditions to it. The other choices describe a system with no repeated funding decisions at all.
questions.hint: Ask how often the money had to be voted again.

questions.stem: During another session, the group considers the argument for transferring the ground fight to allied forces while the sponsoring power supplied air and naval support. Which inference is best supported?

options.text: It spread the cost and the casualties across allies while limiting what the sponsoring power had to commit
It was chosen because the sponsoring power had no capacity to fight any ground war at all
options.misconception: Presents a sharing arrangement as a total incapacity

options.text: It guaranteed that allied forces would outnumber the opposing force in every situation
options.misconception: Assumes a transfer automatically produces superior numbers

options.text: It removed any need for air or naval support from the sponsoring power
options.misconception: Denies the support that any ground campaign required

questions.explanation: The logic of such a transfer is to share weight and losses while keeping the sponsoring power's own commitment small, and it still depends on that power's air and naval support. It says nothing about incapacity or about numerical superiority.
questions.hint: Ask what the sponsoring power gained and kept.

questions.topic: Chinese entry into the Korean War
questions.learningObjective: Compute the growth in an opposing force between two estimates
questions.stem: A revision handout tabulates the size of Chinese forces committed in the war, estimating 200,000 troops by late 1950 and 300,000 by the following spring. By how much did the force grow?

options.text: 100,000 troops, since 300,000 minus 200,000 leaves 100,000
500,000 troops, since the two estimates should be added together
options.misconception: Adds two quantities that must be subtracted

options.text: 150,000 troops, since the later estimate is half again the earlier one
options.misconception: Guesses a fraction without computing the difference

options.text: 200,000 troops, since the first estimate measures the growth better than the difference
options.misconception: Reports the first estimate as the growth

questions.explanation: The increase is 300,000 minus 200,000, which is 100,000 troops, so the commitment roughly doubled over the winter. Adding the two estimates gives a combined total rather than a change.
questions.hint: Subtract the earlier estimate from the later one.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read armistice terms to identify what they settled and what they deferred

stimulus.body: The terms provide that forces on both sides withdraw behind a line running roughly along the 38th parallel, that the line become a demilitarized zone, and that talks on a political settlement continue for years. A closing note records that the parties agreed on the military arrangements but not on the political question.

questions.stem: What do these terms show about the agreement?

options.text: The document stopped the fighting and deferred the political question rather than settling it
The document fixed a permanent political settlement on the northern government's own terms
options.misconception: Reads a deferral as a political settlement

options.text: The document required the total disarmament of both armies within a year
options.misconception: Overstates the demilitarized zone as general disarmament

options.text: The document handed every disputed area to the southern government outright
options.misconception: Contradicts the terms the document records

questions.explanation: The terms are military arrangements, and the closing note says the political question was left open, so the agreement ended the shooting and deferred the dispute. It neither settled the peninsula nor required either army to disband.
questions.hint: Read the closing note about the political question.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what civilian control of war aims means in practice
questions.stem: The revision notes ask what civilian control of war aims means in practice, and why it matters to a conflict. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: Civilian control of war aims means that the purposes a war is fought for are set by elected officials rather than by commanders, and that the military advises within a frame the civilians have fixed. In practice the size and purpose of an operation, the level of force to be used, and the terms on which the war might end are decided in civilian forums, with officers providing judgments about feasibility and cost. The principle matters because a commander's objective is usually to win the engagement, which need not coincide with the political purpose the state has chosen.

questions.explanation: A good answer separates who decides the aims from who advises, and connects the split to the danger of military aims displacing political ones. It should note that advice on feasibility and cost remains essential.
questions.hint: Say who decides and who advises.

questions.learningObjective: Weigh the argument for gradual escalation against its costs
questions.stem: One revision exercise weighs the case for adding forces in small steps against the case for committing quickly and at scale. Which combined judgment is most accurate?

options.text: Gradual steps could be tested and modified, but they also let the conflict widen past its original limits
Gradual steps carried no risk, since each one could be reversed without lasting loss
options.misconception: Presents risk management as risk elimination

options.text: A rapid commitment was clearly better, because it ended the conflict before costs accumulated
options.misconception: Claims a faster path ends a war sooner in every case

options.text: Both tempos guarantee the same result, so the speed of escalation cannot matter
options.misconception: Assumes the tempo of escalation cannot affect the outcome

questions.explanation: Adding measures in steps let each one be judged against the response it produced, which is the argument for caution. The cost was that a war meant to stay limited could grow quietly as each step became the baseline for the next.
questions.hint: Ask what the gradual approach gained and what it allowed to happen.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the aims expected of a bombing campaign against the north

options.text: It was meant to cut the supplies the war effort needed and to show that victory lay out of reach
It was expected to destroy the northern army's fighting units outright in one campaign
options.misconception: Overstates what air power could achieve against an army

options.text: It was expected to force an immediate surrender within a matter of weeks
options.misconception: Assumes bombardment produces instant political surrender

options.text: It was expected to replace ground operations in the near term entirely
options.misconception: Assumes air power made ground operations unnecessary

questions.explanation: The expectation was that damaging industry and transport would squeeze the war effort until continuing cost too much, so the target was the enemy's calculation rather than its army. Bombing alone was never expected to compel surrender at once.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about why reported casualty figures cannot simply be added up
questions.stem: During a later session, the group asks why the enemy dead reported for separate battles cannot be totalled into a reliable figure for the war. Which explanation is best?

options.text: Each figure is an estimate made at one place and one moment, and the two sides count on different bases
The two sides deliberately published matching figures so that neither appeared weaker
options.misconception: Invents a matching rule that does not exist

options.text: Bodies could only be counted once a war had been formally concluded and the ground was clear
options.misconception: Gets the timing of counting wrong

options.text: A single agency produced the figures on both sides, so the totals agree by construction
options.misconception: Contradicts the fact that the two sides counted separately

questions.explanation: Each reported figure is bound to a particular moment, place, and set of counting rules, and the two sides used different ones, so summing them compounds the errors. Nothing in the practice requires matching publication or a single collecting agency.
questions.hint: Ask what each individual figure actually covers.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the share of war funding directed to the military
questions.stem: A revision handout lists war-related funding for one year: the legislature approved 47 billion dollars, of which 33 billion covered the military and 14 billion covered economic assistance and foreign aid. What share went to the military?

options.text: About 70 percent, since 33 of 47 billion is close to seven tenths
About 30 percent, since 14 of 47 billion is roughly three tenths
options.misconception: Reports the smaller share as the main figure

options.text: About 50 percent, since the two categories are of similar size
options.misconception: Assumes similar lines mean an even split

options.text: About 100 percent, since all of the war funding was military in the end
options.misconception: Ignores the second category entirely

questions.hint: Divide the military figure by the approved total.

options.misconception: Misreads the focus of the proposal

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Chinese entry into the Korean War
questions.learningObjective: Explain how stated reasons and strategic reality can both hold
questions.stem: The revision notes ask how China's stated reasons for entering the war and the conditions of its intervention can both be true at once. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: China's leaders described their intervention as a response to attacks across the border and to a call for assistance, and they held their forces back until those calls were made, which kept the intervention defensible in law and in argument. The conduct matched the description in some respects, since the entry was presented as defensive and stayed below the parallel, but the deployment was also a response to a war that had widened in ways China had not chosen. A good answer holds the stated justification and the strategic reality at once rather than dismissing one as a pretext.

questions.explanation: A strong answer sets out the stated justification and the timing that protected it, then shows how the strategic situation also shaped the decision. It should avoid declaring the stated reasons simply false.
questions.hint: Hold both the public account and the circumstances together.

options.misconception: Reads a deferral as a completed settlement

options.text: The armistice and the later talks produced the same political result in the end

options.text: The armistice ended the war, so the later negotiations were unnecessary
options.misconception: Contradicts the fact that negotiations continued for years

questions.explanation: The armistice settled where the front would stand and left the political dispute open, and the long subsequent talks confirm that the dispute was never closed. Treating the truce as a settlement misreads the whole sequence.
questions.hint: Ask what the later talks were about if the question was settled.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how appropriations control gave civilians leverage
questions.stem: The revision notes ask why control of the money gave civilian leaders leverage over military plans. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: Military plans need money to be more than plans, and money has to be voted on a schedule, so civilian officials acquire leverage at each renewal: they can slow an operation by delaying a vote, reduce its scope by cutting specific lines, or attach conditions to the funds. Legislators can also hold hearings that force assumptions the military has not tested in public to be defended. The leverage is not unlimited, since a government that refuses to fund a war eventually has to accept its demands or end it, but it is real and it shapes what gets attempted.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains the link between money and action, lists the forms that leverage takes, and notes its limits. It should avoid presenting the power as absolute or as operating only once.
questions.hint: Ask what the money controls and where it is decided.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the fraction of stated war aims that were dropped
questions.stem: A revision group's chart lists five war aims set by civilian officials at different moments, and records that the military's briefings addressed three of them while two were dropped from later briefings. What fraction of the aims were dropped?

options.text: Two fifths, since 2 of the 5 stated aims were dropped
Three fifths, since the military addressed only 3 of the 5 aims
options.misconception: Reports aims not addressed as aims dropped

options.text: One fifth, since only one aim survived every briefing
options.misconception: Misreads the addressing of aims as their survival

options.text: All five, since an aim missing from a briefing is no longer an active aim
options.misconception: Treats silence in a briefing as formal abandonment

questions.explanation: Two of the five stated aims were dropped, which is two fifths, while the three that were addressed are a separate count of a different thing. Omission from a briefing shows only that the aim was not discussed, not that it was formally abandoned.
questions.hint: Divide the number dropped by the number stated.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read a policy sequence for the difference between a halt and a reversal

stimulus.body: The document lists the measures in order: advisers, then a bombing campaign, then large ground deployments, then a wider bombing campaign, then further ground units, and finally a halt in the bombing while the ground deployments continued at their existing strength. A note adds that the commitments of earlier allies were retained.

questions.stem: What does the final step show about the pattern of escalation?

options.text: That the policy could be altered in one dimension while being held in another, so it was not a single line
That the policy was reversed entirely once the bombing was stopped
options.misconception: Reads a partial change as a full reversal

options.text: That the ground deployments were withdrawn along with the bombing
options.misconception: Contradicts the document on continued deployments

options.text: That the sequence had no pattern, since each measure was unrelated to the others
options.misconception: Denies the clear ordering the document shows

questions.explanation: Stopping the bombing while keeping the ground deployments shows the policy moving in one area and holding in another, which is what an incremental approach looks like in practice. It is neither a complete reversal nor an unrelated set of decisions.
questions.hint: Compare what changed with what stayed the same.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why expectations about bombing outran its results
questions.stem: The revision notes ask why the hopes attached to bombing the north proved larger than its effects. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The campaign was expected to work on two audiences at once, the government in the north and the governments watching the war elsewhere, and both judgments proved too confident. Against the north the expectation was that damage to industry and transport would squeeze the war effort until continuing became too expensive, but the country rebuilt, moved work around, and kept going. Abroad the expectation was that resolve would reassure allies and warn opponents, but visible destruction produced pressure for the war to end rather than awe. Both failures came from treating material damage as though it directly produced political decisions.

questions.explanation: A good answer examines both audiences the campaign was aimed at and shows why the expected political effect did not follow from the damage. It should avoid claiming the campaign had no effect of any kind.
questions.hint: Check the expectations against the two audiences involved.

questions.learningObjective: Compare the counting practices of the two sides in a war
questions.stem: One revision exercise compares how the two opposing sides counted the dead in the same war. Which combined judgment is most accurate?

options.text: Each side counted in ways that suited its argument, so the totals are estimates with a direction of bias
Each side used identical methods, so their totals should agree closely
options.misconception: Assumes identical counting methods on both sides

options.text: Only the side that fought on the ground could count casualties at all
options.misconception: Assumes only ground forces could count casualties

options.text: The two sides deliberately set matching totals to avoid political embarrassment
options.misconception: Invents a coordinating rule between the two sides

questions.explanation: Each side had reasons to inflate, minimise, or reclassify the losses it reported, and the counting rules differed, so published totals carry a direction of bias and are best read as informed estimates. They were neither coordinated nor produced by identical methods.
questions.hint: Ask what each side had to gain from its own figures.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how appropriations power operates without ending a war
questions.stem: A revision group asks how civilian control of war money could be used without cutting a war to nothing. Which answer is best?

options.text: Through conditions, hearings, and delays that narrow and slow a campaign without terminating it
By automatically expiring appropriations after a year, which forced a new vote on every need
options.misconception: Asserts a fixed expiry rule the process does not have

options.text: By applying only to peacetime establishments, since wartime funds could not be touched
options.misconception: Restricts the power to peacetime budgets

options.text: By becoming irrelevant once a war was voted, since no further funding question could arise
options.misconception: Contradicts the repeated funding decisions the power depends on

questions.explanation: The leverage lay in the repeated funding decisions, which let civilian bodies attach conditions, demand explanations, and slow the rate of spending on a campaign they did not approve outright. Nothing in the process gave every appropriation a fixed one-year life or excluded wartime funds.
questions.hint: Ask what can be done with money that is approved but constrained.

It freed the sponsoring power from any dependence on allied governments

options.text: It guaranteed allied commitment for as long as the sponsoring power wanted it

options.misconception: Denies the influence that followed from reliance

About 120 percent, since 240,000 is more than double 200,000
options.misconception: Compares the total with the first figure and misreads it

options.text: About 5 percent, since 40,000 divided by 800,000 is one twentieth
options.misconception: Divides by a figure eight times too large

options.misconception: Confuses the size of the addition with the rate of growth

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read a document for the difference between a halt and a settlement

stimulus.body: The document records that the truce was signed in July 1953, that a conference on the political issue was held afterward, and that the two sides continued to disagree over what the conference should decide. It notes that both governments used the continuing talks to press their own positions.

questions.stem: What does this document show?

options.text: That the fighting was ended while the question that had caused it was left open
That the conference settled the political question within a matter of months
options.misconception: Claims a settlement the document does not record

options.text: That agreeing to talk was itself a form of political recognition of the other side
options.misconception: Overstates what agreeing to talk implied

options.text: That the war resumed because the truce failed to hold
options.misconception: Invents a resumption the document does not describe

questions.explanation: A signed truce and later talks that continued without agreement show the fighting stopped while the underlying dispute stayed unresolved. Entering a conference was not the same as recognising the other side's claim, and the document records no resumption.
questions.hint: Compare the end of the fighting with the fate of the dispute.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why civilian control of war aims was contested in practice
questions.stem: The revision notes ask why the principle of civilian control of war aims was often contested in practice. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The principle is clear when the government and the military agree, and contested when officers judge that the stated aims cannot be reached without steps the government has not authorised. A commander's professional objective is to win the engagement, and pressure to achieve the political aim quickly can produce proposals that enlarge the war beyond what civilians intended. Civilian officials face their own difficulty, since the costs of a war fall on the public while the reputational cost of reversing policy falls on the administration, and that tension makes civilian control look like hesitation.

questions.explanation: A good answer identifies the gap between the political aim and the military recommendation, and shows that civilians face their own pressures too. It should not present the tension as a contest between good and bad actors.
questions.hint: Ask what each side wants from the same decision.

questions.learningObjective: Compare two explanations for the pattern of gradual escalation
questions.stem: One revision exercise weighs two explanations for gradual escalation, one stressing the testing of the opponent's response and the other stressing domestic reasons for avoiding a broad commitment. Which combined judgment is most accurate?

options.text: The two explanations draw on different evidence and can both be part of what drove the pattern
One explanation credits the steps with defeating the opponent and the other blames them for the war's length
options.misconception: Presents two different arguments as a judgment and its opposite

options.text: Both explanations reduce to the claim that commanders wanted to avoid civilian oversight
options.misconception: Reduces a strategic and a political question to one narrow concern

options.text: The two explanations are the same argument stated in different words
options.misconception: Treats distinct explanations as identical

questions.explanation: Testing an opponent's reaction and managing domestic politics are distinct kinds of evidence for why a government adds measures slowly, and both can be operating at once. Neither explanation is the other's opposite, and neither reduces to a complaint about civilian oversight.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of evidence each explanation rests on.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the limits of a bombing campaign against an industrial base

Its effect was limited only because the aircraft used could not carry enough fuel to reach the targets
options.misconception: Reduces the question to equipment range rather than results

options.text: Its effect was limited because the targets were too small for any bomb to matter at all
options.misconception: Treats every target as insignificant in scale

options.text: Its effect was limited because the northern government surrendered before the campaign ended
options.misconception: Contradicts the campaign's actual duration and outcome

questions.explanation: Bombing works on the northern war effort only if the damage is hard to repair or relocate, and the economy's ability to shift production was the serious question observers raised. Aircraft range mattered practically, and no surrender ended the campaign.
questions.hint: Ask what the bombs had to make impossible to undo.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about comparing estimates drawn from different periods
questions.stem: In a later session, students ask about the effect of pauses in fighting on the estimates that are later produced. Which explanation is best?

options.text: Estimates cover periods with different conditions, so a figure for one cannot simply be added to another
Estimates are reliable only when they cover the whole war, so figures for any shorter period are worthless
options.misconception: Renders partial estimates useless in every case

options.text: A pause in fighting makes later estimates more accurate, because counting becomes easier afterwards
options.misconception: Assumes counting conditions improve after a halt

options.text: Estimates are gathered by a single international body, so figures for different periods always match
options.misconception: Assumes a single collecting body for the figures

questions.explanation: A figure for an active phase and a figure for a quiet phase rest on different evidence and different conditions, so adding them can double-count or leave gaps. Partial estimates are still useful, and they are not all produced by one body.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the increase in annual war spending from a series
questions.stem: A revision handout lists annual war spending across four years as 12 billion, 19 billion, 28 billion, and 41 billion dollars. What was the increase between the first year and the last?

options.text: 29 billion dollars, since 41 minus 12 leaves 29
53 billion dollars, since the four figures should be added together
options.misconception: Adds four figures instead of finding one difference

options.text: About 3.4 times, since 41 divided by 12 is roughly 3.4
options.misconception: Reports a ratio when an amount was asked for

options.text: 29 percent, since 29 over 12 is the growth rate
options.misconception: Reports a rate when an amount was asked for

questions.explanation: The question asks for an amount, and the difference between the first and last years is 41 minus 12, which is 29 billion dollars. The ratio of 3.4 and the rate of roughly 242 percent are different measurements of the same series.
questions.hint: Subtract the first year's figure from the last year's.

questions.topic: Handing the ground war to allies
questions.learningObjective: Read a document on the distribution of costs under an allied ground war

stimulus.body: The note records that allied forces bore most of the ground casualties while the sponsoring power supplied the air and naval support, and that the arrangement allowed the sponsoring power to keep its own ground commitments small. It adds that the political effect at home of a low American casualty count was a stated aim of the arrangement.

questions.stem: What does this document show about the arrangement?

options.text: It exchanged the sponsor's ground presence for allied manpower at a lower political and economic cost
It withdrew the sponsoring power entirely from the military effort of the war
options.misconception: Overstates the reduction to complete withdrawal

options.text: It had allied forces fight without any support from the sponsoring power
options.misconception: Contradicts the document on support provided

options.text: It produced equal casualty shares among all the participating countries
options.misconception: Contradicts the document on the distribution of casualties

questions.explanation: Allied forces supplied the manpower and therefore most of the ground losses, while the sponsor provided air and naval power and kept its own troops lightly committed, which suited the stated aim of a low domestic casualty count. It was a division of roles, not a withdrawal.
questions.hint: Ask who supplied the manpower and who supplied the support.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Chinese entry into the Korean War
questions.learningObjective: Explain how Chinese entry changed the scale of the war
questions.stem: The revision notes ask what changed about the scale and character of the war once Chinese forces entered. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: Before the Chinese intervention the United Nations coalition was defending a perimeter in the far southeast while the approach to the capital was still open. Chinese forces gave the north a depth of manpower that let it sustain a far larger ground offensive through the winter, so the coalition was pushed back to a perimeter near the original border and allied planners began to fear a campaign they might not be able to contain. The entry also changed the political arithmetic of the conflict, because what had been a regional war became a confrontation that could draw in major powers directly.

questions.explanation: A good answer traces the added manpower, the large northern offensive, the coalition's retreat, and the new risk of an unlimited campaign. It should also note the political shift from a regional to a great-power confrontation.
questions.hint: Follow the manpower, the offensive, and the response.

The region was legally at peace, because a halt had been signed and observed
options.misconception: Treats a halt in fighting as a general state of peace

options.text: The question of the peninsula's political future had been permanently set aside
options.misconception: Treats a deferred question as permanently closed

options.misconception: Invents an enforcement mandate the record does not contain

questions.explanation: A halt without a treaty suspended the fighting but left the dispute unresolved and therefore resumable, and the long negotiations that followed confirm that the questions stayed live. Neither a general state of peace nor a permanent settlement followed from the agreement.
questions.hint: Ask what a halt leaves available for the future.

The military decides whenever the civilian aims are judged unachievable
options.misconception: Makes the military's judgment final on civilian questions

A slow buildup makes ending the war easier, because the public grows tired of one small step at a time
options.misconception: Treats war weariness as easing the political problem

options.text: The tempo made no difference, since the length of the war was set by the opponent alone
options.misconception: Denies the domestic link between commitments and duration

options.text: A fast buildup would have made ending the war harder, because the commitments would arrive at once
options.misconception: Reverses which tempo creates the harder exit

questions.hint: Ask what each new commitment does to the next decision.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the tonnage directed at a target category

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a recorded campaign figure as a convention-bound estimate

stimulus.body: The study recorded 137,000 enemy dead in one phase of the campaign, and the opposing side published a different figure for the same phase. The study notes that the two totals used different categories, since one of them included unconfirmed reports and the other counted confirmed casualties only.

questions.stem: What does this recorded figure show?

options.text: That a single campaign total is a convention-bound estimate rather than a direct observation
That one of the two published totals must be entirely false
options.misconception: Assumes disagreement means falsity

options.text: That the two totals measure different events and so cannot be compared at all
options.misconception: Overstates the difference as measuring different events

options.text: That military studies do not attempt casualty figures for campaigns
options.misconception: Contradicts the study's own recorded figure

questions.explanation: A stated total depends on the counting rules in force, including whether unconfirmed reports are included, so two totals for the same phase can differ without either being a falsehood. The figure is a measured estimate, not an observed count.
questions.hint: Ask what the rules for counting included.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how war spending interacts with the wider budget
questions.stem: The revision notes ask how war spending interacts with the ordinary budget and with politics at home. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: War appropriations are large enough to dominate the ordinary budget, which means money has to be taken from programmes that were already planned, and those cuts are decided at the same time as the war's costs are approved. That makes the war's price visible in domestic terms rather than as an abstraction, and it gives opponents of the war a way to argue about it in the legislature. At the same time, because one vote carries both the war and the non-war items, the political fate of each becomes entangled with the fate of the other, which makes a clean separation hard to argue.

questions.explanation: A good answer shows how war money competes with other programmes, why that makes the war's cost politically visible, and how the bundled vote entangles the two. It should avoid treating the budget as a neutral accounting exercise.
questions.hint: Ask what the war money is taken away from and how it is voted.

questions.hint: Ask what the sponsor was still doing and what it was avoiding.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read a policy statement for the logic of reversible steps

stimulus.body: The statement says that each new measure should be small enough to be reversed, that the aim was to press the opponent rather than to decide the outcome, and that any expansion should follow only if the pressure already applied had failed to produce movement. questions.stem: What is the logic of the policy as the statement presents it?

options.text: That limited and reversible steps keep options open and avoid the risks of a large commitment
That each step was intended as the decisive one, with later steps reserved for failure
options.misconception: Reverses the stated purpose of the limited steps

options.text: That the policy required the largest possible commitment at the first opportunity
options.misconception: Contradicts the preference for small reversible measures

options.text: That the policy's purpose was to make the war unwinnable for the opponent by definition
options.misconception: Misreads pressuring as a declared intention to defeat

questions.explanation: The statement describes a method: keep each measure small enough to undo, use it to press rather than to decide, and add further measures only if the pressure has failed. That is a theory of graduated pressure, not a plan for one decisive blow.
questions.hint: Ask what each step was meant to accomplish and to leave open.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the political effects of a bombing campaign in both directions
questions.stem: The revision notes ask how a bombing campaign against the north shaped the diplomatic picture. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The campaign was expected to strengthen the government that authorised it by showing resolve at home and to allies abroad, and it did generate support in some capitals and a degree of political constraint on the other side. It also produced the opposite effect elsewhere, because the visible destruction of a civilian industrial base made the war look less like the defence of a small country and more like an assault on a population, which strained support in the countries whose cooperation the campaign depended on. The campaign therefore shaped the war politically in both directions at the same time.

questions.explanation: A good answer weighs the intended and the unintended political effects together, and it links the strain on allied support to the campaign's dependence on that support. It should avoid presenting the effects as all in one direction.
questions.hint: Ask who was persuaded and who was disturbed.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Recommend how casualty figures should be cited in study
questions.stem: One revision exercise asks how a study group should treat casualty figures when it writes up a war's human cost. Which combined judgment is most accurate?

options.text: Cite them as informed estimates with a stated range, and say who produced them and what they counted
Cite the single most frequently quoted figure, because a range invites doubt about the whole account
options.misconception: Treats a single number as stronger than a documented range

options.text: Avoid casualty figures entirely, because every estimate of this kind is unreliable
options.misconception: Overstates the unreliability of published estimates

options.text: Use whichever figure comes from the side whose account the group finds more credible
options.misconception: Chooses figures by preference rather than by provenance

questions.explanation: The honest form is to give the estimate, the range, and the source, so that a reader can judge the counting rules behind the number. A single figure, no figure, and a figure chosen for political preference all hide the uncertainty instead of describing it.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader needs in order to judge the figure.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a specific appropriation line gives leverage over a program
questions.stem: A revision group asks what a defense appropriation line for one specific program allows legislators to do. Which answer is best?

options.text: Question and restrict that particular activity without voting against the whole of the war
Approve or reject the entire military program as a single indivisible item
options.misconception: Assumes appropriations are all-or-nothing votes

options.text: Nothing, since money cannot be separated from the policy that requested it
options.misconception: Contradicts the line-item practice the power depends on

options.text: End the program automatically at the close of the fiscal year without further action
options.misconception: Adds an automatic lapse the process does not provide

questions.explanation: Because money is voted in lines, a legislature can pick out one activity and question, delay, or trim it while leaving the wider war programme intact, which is the practical form of the power of the purse. It does not create automatic cancellations or all-or-nothing votes.
questions.hint: Ask what a single line lets them pick out.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Handing the ground war to allies
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the risk of depending on allied ground forces
questions.stem: In a further session, students consider the risks of relying on allies to fight the ground war. Which inference is best supported?

options.text: Allied commitment rests on allied domestic politics, which can shift faster than the war's demands
Allies have no domestic politics capable of influencing a war they are fighting
options.misconception: Denies the political constraints on allies

options.text: Reliance on allies removes the sponsoring power's need for a ground capability of any kind
options.misconception: Overstates what the arrangement removes

options.text: Allied forces will always fight exactly as the sponsoring power intends them to
options.misconception: Assumes perfect alignment between sponsor and ally

questions.explanation: Allied governments must answer to their own publics and parliaments, so their willingness to keep fighting can change faster than the campaign requires, which is a real risk for a sponsor. It does not remove the need for some ground capability, and perfect alignment cannot be assumed.
questions.hint: Ask who an allied government must answer to at home.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Chinese entry into the Korean War
questions.learningObjective: Compute the monthly increase in losses from two rates
questions.stem: A revision handout states that in the three months after Chinese forces entered, coalition losses rose from about 3,000 a month to about 15,000 a month. What was the monthly increase?

options.text: 12,000 a month, since 15,000 minus 3,000 leaves 12,000
18,000 a month, since the two rates should be added together
options.misconception: Adds two rates instead of taking the difference

options.text: 5,000 a month, since a fivefold increase implies a difference of 5,000
options.misconception: Misreads the multiplier as the amount of increase

options.text: 3,000 a month, since the earlier rate sets the monthly figure
options.misconception: Reports the earlier rate as the increase

questions.explanation: The monthly increase is 15,000 minus 3,000, which is 12,000, while the fivefold description states only the ratio between the two rates. A difference has to be taken between the two levels themselves.
questions.hint: Subtract the earlier monthly rate from the later one.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read a document about the intended duration of a pause in fighting

stimulus.body: The document records a remark that the pause in fighting was the first in a series of pauses, that the parties had agreed to a longer pause of two years rather than to a permanent settlement, and that the line separating the forces was to be supervised while it held.

questions.stem: Reading this document, what can be concluded about the pause the parties agreed?

options.text: The arrangement was explicitly temporary and was meant to be revisited before it expired
The parties had already agreed a final and permanent end to the fighting
options.misconception: Reverses the stated length and intent of the pause

options.text: The pause was imposed by an international body against the parties' own wishes
options.misconception: Invents outside compulsion the document does not mention

options.text: The document shows the fighting continued throughout the whole period of the pause
options.misconception: Contradicts the pause itself

questions.explanation: A pause of a defined length agreed in place of a permanent settlement shows the arrangement was deliberately temporary and revisitable. The parties made the choice themselves, and the pause means the fighting was not continuing during it.
questions.hint: Ask what the parties agreed instead of a permanent settlement.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how civilian control shapes the drafting of war aims
questions.stem: The revision notes ask how the principle of civilian control shaped the way war aims were written. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: A war aim written for civilian decision has to state a political purpose rather than a military position, because a civilian audience asks what the fighting is for and what success would look like, while a commander needs the same question answered in terms of terrain, forces, and timing. Drafting aims in political terms forces the argument about objectives into a forum where it can be debated and amended, and it makes the point at which the war should stop a matter of definition rather than of circumstance. The drafting itself therefore settles a good deal of the war's direction before a shot is fired.

questions.explanation: A good answer links the audience for an aim to the terms in which it is phrased, and shows the drafting as the point where the war's purpose becomes contestable. It should avoid treating civilian drafting as a formality.
questions.hint: Ask what an audience needs an aim to say.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compare the pattern of escalation across two conflicts
questions.stem: One revision exercise compares escalation in one conflict with escalation in another. Which combined judgment is most accurate?

options.text: In both cases each step added a new instrument while the earlier ones continued, so escalation compounded
In one case the steps replaced each other and in the other they accumulated, so the two cannot be compared
options.misconception: Assumes the two cases must be incomparable

options.text: One conflict escalated for strategic reasons and the other for domestic political reasons, which explains the difference
options.misconception: Presents a difference of motive as the whole comparison

options.text: Neither conflict escalated, since the word describes only the rhetoric of officials
options.misconception: Denies the observable pattern of added measures

questions.explanation: In both conflicts the pattern is the same: new instruments were added while the earlier ones were kept, so the pressure on the opponent compounded rather than being exchanged. A difference in motive between the two cases is compatible with that shared pattern.
questions.hint: Ask what happened to the earlier measures in each case.
